extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, classics, and ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and regulations for founding and maintaining an ideal city (esp. the guardian class) as argued in Plato's Republic Book IV. Covers selection, education, property, habits, virtues (wisdom, courage, temperance, justice), and institutional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians selected by nature and maintained by rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers must anxiously guard the purity of the race; observe what elements mingle in offspring and degrade or elevate children according to their natural composition (gold, silver, brass, iron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example/anti-pattern: A golden parent may have a silver son or vice versa; if an offspring has an admixture making him inferior, the rulers must not be pitiful but reassign the child to the class for which nature intended him. The aim is to ensure each individual performs the work suited to his nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a civic 'noble lie' to secure social cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Invent a tale (the story of metals in souls) to make citizens believe in differentiated origins so they will care more for the city and for one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Accept that the present generation may not believe it, but tell it and instill it in their sons and posterity. Purpose is social cohesion and willingness to perform one’s assigned role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians’ habitations must be soldierly, not mercantile
rubrics_metrics.description: Dwellings must shield them against cold and heat and be 'houses of soldiers', not of shop-keepers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: Their living arrangements should not resemble private households that foster private wealth or commerce; communal/military-style living preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians must not own private property beyond necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: None of them should have any property of his own beyond what is absolutely necessary; they should not have private houses or stores closed against any one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: They receive a fixed rate of pay enough to meet yearly expenses and no more; they live together in mess like soldiers to prevent accumulation of wealth that leads to corruption or tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on touching or possessing gold and silver
rubrics_metrics.description: They alone of all the citizens may not touch or handle silver or gold, or be under the same roof with them, or wear them, or drink from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: 'The diviner metal is within them' so they have no need for corrupting common metal; gold/silver has been the source of many unholy deeds. Anti-pattern: Allowing guardians to handle precious metals risks their becoming housekeepers, husbandmen, enemies, and tyrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians live communally and receive modest fixed pay
rubrics_metrics.description: Their provisions should be only such as are required by trained warriors; they should agree to receive from the citizens a fixed rate of pay, enough to meet the expenses of the year and no more; and they will go to mess and live together like soldiers in a camp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: Promote temperance and courage; prevent pursuit of private luxuries (mistresses, journeys) that undermine virtue and duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent guardians from acquiring homes, lands, or money
rubrics_metrics.description: Should they ever acquire homes or lands or moneys of their own, they will become housekeepers and husbandmen instead of guardians, enemies and tyrants instead of allies of the other citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: Allowing private accumulation leads to hatred, plotting, terror of internal enemies, and ruin of the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as the central legislative instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Education and nurture are the one sufficient thing to which attention of rulers should be directed; 'good nurture and education implant good constitutions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: True education civilizes and humanizes guardians; direction of education determines future life. Legislating less about minutiae is acceptable if education is right, because citizens will find necessary regulations themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve music and gymnastics in original form; ban musical innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Music and gymnastic must be preserved in their original form, and no innovation made. Any musical innovation is full of danger to the whole State and ought to be prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Changes in musical modes accompany changes in fundamental laws and lead to moral and constitutional decay. Anti-pattern: Praising 'new kind of song' leads to lawlessness that penetrates manners, customs, contracts, and laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train youth strictly from the first; early education fixes character
rubrics_metrics.description: Youth should be trained from the first in a stricter system; the direction in which education starts a man will determine his future life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: Dyers prepare the ground so the dye 'takes' permanently; similarly music/gymnastics prepare guardians to take the dye of the laws and preserve correct opinions under pleasure, pain, desire, or fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians prepared for war by encampment and sacrifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a spot to encamp from which they can suppress insurrection and defend against external enemies; there let them encamp, sacrifice to the proper gods, and prepare their dwellings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational: Practical military organization, rituals, and suitably placed habitations support the guardians’ role as defenders and maintainers of order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against corruption from wealth and poverty
rubrics_metrics.description: Two causes of deterioration of the arts (and morals) are wealth and poverty: wealth breeds luxury and indolence, poverty breeds meanness and viciousness; both cause degeneration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians must watch against these evils; social arrangements should avoid extremes of wealth/power consolidation that threaten the State's stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the size of the State to preserve unity and self-sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow the State to increase so far as is consistent with unity; the proper limit is a State that is one and self-sufficing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: Excessive expansion harms unity; a modest, self-sufficient State of well-ordered citizens can be greater 'in deed and truth' than larger, divided polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social mobility by degrading/elevating offspring by nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Duty of degrading the offspring of guardians when inferior, and of elevating into the rank of guardians the offspring of lower classes when naturally superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: Ensure every individual is put to the use for which nature intended him — 'one man should practise one thing only' — to maintain harmony and efficiency in the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers’ knowledge (wisdom) must concern the whole State
rubrics_metrics.description: Wisdom in the State is the knowledge that counsels about the whole: the knowledge of the guardians, not of craftsmen. This kind of knowledge gives a city the title of good in counsel and truly wise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: Guardians should be few in number but possess comprehensive knowledge to guide the State; specialized crafts do not confer the kind of wisdom needed for rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage as correct and stable opinion about fear (not brute courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage is preservation under all circumstances of the opinion about the things to be feared and not to be feared which the law implants; it is not mere uninstructed or brute courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training in music and gymnastics prepares the soul to hold these impressions 'fast' so that pleasure, fear, or desire do not wash them away. Anti-pattern: Courage of a wild beast or slave is not the civic courage meant by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance (self-mastery) as harmony across classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance is the ordering or controlling of certain pleasures and desires; it is a kind of harmony and symphony — agreement among superior and inferior about who should rule; it extends through the whole State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance is realized when the better principle has the worse under control; it is not confined to one part but runs through all classes producing social harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice defined as each doing one’s own work
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is the principle that one man should practise one thing only and do his own business, and not be a busybody; justice is doing one's own work in the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the culmination of the inquiry: justice in the State corresponds to the proper ordering and division of roles, each part performing its function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation should avoid over-regulation of minor matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Little wisdom in legislating minutiae of dress, manners, market dealings etc.; good men will devise necessary regulations themselves, and many particulars will naturally flow from prior regulations if education is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical stance: Legislator should focus on the great matters; minutiae are better handled by customs and the education-instilled character of citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious rites and the greatest matters entrusted to deity
rubrics_metrics.description: Institution of temples, sacrifices, rites for the dead, and service of gods are beyond founders’ expertise and should be entrusted to Apollo (the deity) or the appropriate religious interpreters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges limits of human legislation in sacred observances; legislators should not arrogate religious authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of flatterers and political corrupters
rubrics_metrics.description: States where citizens are forbidden to alter constitution may still be corrupted by ministers who flatter the multitude and anticipate their humours; such men may be mistaken for statesmen and are dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: Praising those who pander to the crowd; true legislators should recognize and avoid such flatterers who destabilize constitutions by appealing to popular vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good order is self-reinforcing if founded well
rubrics_metrics.description: If the State is once started well, it moves with accumulating force: good nurture implants good constitutions, which then improve the breed and perpetuate virtue across generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for policy: Invest in foundational education/arrangements early; positive feedback will sustain and improve the polity over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cultural and legal signals to attract allies in war
rubrics_metrics.description: Because guardians lack gold, they might send embassies to richer cities offering spoils to recruit allies: 'Silver and gold we neither have nor are permitted to have, but you may; do you therefore come and help us in war, and take the spoils of the other city.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic guidance: Present guardians as lean, wiry dogs whose martial skill but lack of loot makes them attractive allies to rich states seeking plunder; leverages reputation and realistic bargaining.
